identity.title: Compact molecular gas emission in local LIRGs among low- and high-z galaxies

paper_type_evidence.quote: We present new CO(2-1) observations of a representative sample of 24 local (z$<$0.02) luminous infrared galaxies (LIRGs) at high spatial resolution ($<$100 pc) from the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA).

We obtained the CO(2–1) line and the continuum at 247 GHz ($\sim$1.3 mm) emissions of a sample of 18 individual local LIRGs observed with ALMA between August 2014 and August 2018, using the Band 6 from the project 2017.1.00255.S

findings_qualitative.value: Local LIRGs have a very compact cold molecular gas distribution (median R_CO ~ 0.7 kpc), which is ~2 times smaller than the H-alpha ionized gas and ~3.5 times smaller than the stellar size.

evidence.quote: LIRGs show an extremely compact cold molecular gas distribution (median R$_{CO}$ $\sim$0.7 kpc), which is a factor 2 smaller than the ionized gas (median R$_{H\alpha}$$\sim$1.4 kpc), and 3.5 times smaller than the stellar size (median R$_{star}$$\sim$2.4 kpc).

findings_qualitative.value: There is no relation between the molecular gas size R_CO and the morphological/dynamical class of the LIRGs.

evidence.loc: No relation between the molecular size and the morphological type
evidence.quote: We can thus claim that no relation has been found between the molecular size, R$_{CO}$, and the galaxy types.

findings_qualitative.value: LIRGs hosting an AGN have median molecular gas sizes a factor of ~2 larger than LIRGs without an AGN (KS test p-value = 0.08).

evidence.loc: The impact of AGN on the molecular gas
evidence.quote: In our particular case, larger (median) molecular radii by a factor of 2 are derived when considering galaxies with an AGN

evidence.loc: The impact of AGN on the molecular gas
evidence.quote: For the molecular emission the test suggests that the two subsamples (AGN *versus* non-AGN) are not drawn from the same parent sample (p-value=0.08)

findings_qualitative.value: When ionized gas is traced by near-IR Pa-alpha (less affected by dust extinction than H-alpha), its effective radius agrees tightly with the CO(2-1) effective radius.

evidence.quote: In this case we found a tight correlation between the two tracers: indeed, for this subsample (see § [4.2.3](#EXTINC)) the effective radius derived for CO(2–1) emission are very similar to that derived for the Pa$\alpha$ emission.

findings_qualitative.value: Local LIRGs share similar stellar masses, stellar sizes, and molecular sizes with local ETGs, while being ~6 times more compact in CO and ~1.6 times more compact in stellar size than local Spirals.

evidence.quote: LIRGs are indistinguishable from ETGs in the M$_{star}$-R$_{star}$ plane, sharing a similar range in their stellar mass and size. However, LIRGs have a stellar host more compact than that of local Spirals, by a factor 1.6.
the molecular size of LIRG is $\sim$6 times more compact than local Spirals of similar stellar mass, while similar to local ETGs, although characterized by higher SFR.

findings_qualitative.value: Local LIRGs have stellar masses and sizes similar to intermediate-redshift (z~1-4) MS SFGs, but their molecular gas distributions are ~2.6 times smaller than high-z MS SFGs and ~7.8 times smaller than high-z SMGs.

evidence.quote: LIRGs, representing the population of bursty above-*MS* SFGs at low-z, appear to be similar to the bulk population of *MS* SFGs at intermediate redshfit (z$\sim$1-4) in terms of the stellar mass and the size of their host galaxies;
LIRGs appear to be more compact than high-z SFGs in their molecular gas distribution (factor 2.6 smaller) while having a slightly smaller size (factor 1.3 smaller) in their stellar host.

claims.hypothesis: The spatial extent of cold molecular gas (potential star formation) in local LIRGs differs from their ionized gas (ongoing star formation) and stellar host sizes.
claims.experiment: Measure curve-of-growth effective radii of CO(2-1) and 1.3 mm continuum from high-resolution (<100 pc) ALMA images of 24 local LIRGs and compare with VIMOS H-alpha, HST Pa-alpha, and 2MASS K-band sizes.
claims.result: Median R_CO = 0.67 kpc (mean 0.66 +/- 0.33 kpc), compared to median R_Halpha = 1.22 kpc (1.4 kpc) and median R_star = 2.41 kpc (median R_star/R_CO = 3.3 +/- 1.0); for the Pa-alpha subsample, median R_CO = 0.79 kpc and R_Pa_alpha = 0.68 kpc.
claims.finding: Cold molecular gas in local LIRGs is strongly centrally concentrated within the central kpc, ~3.5 times more compact than the stellar host and ~2 times more compact than optical H-alpha emission (though similar in size to near-IR Pa-alpha).

evidence.quote: LIRGs show an extremely compact cold molecular gas distribution (median R$_{CO}$ $\sim$0.7 kpc), which is a factor 2 smaller than the ionized gas (median R$_{H\alpha}$$\sim$1.4 kpc), and 3.5 times smaller than the stellar size (median R$_{star}$$\sim$2.4 kpc).

evidence.loc: Ionized (H$\alpha$) and stellar emissions in LIRGs: relations with the molecular distribution
evidence.quote: The ratio between the stellar and the molecular CO sizes give a (median) value of R$_{star}$/R$_{CO}$ = 3.3$\pm$1.0, while the ionized and molecular gas shows more similar values (R$_{H\alpha}$/R$_{CO}$ = 1.5$\pm$0.8).

claims.hypothesis: The molecular gas size R_CO in local LIRGs depends on their morphological/dynamical interaction class.
claims.experiment: Classify the 24 LIRGs into isolated rotating disks (0 RD), perturbed disks (0 PD), interacting systems (1), and mergers (2) using Spitzer/HST morphology and H-alpha/CO kinematics, and compare R_CO across classes.
claims.result: Mean (median) R_CO is 0.73 (0.73) kpc for 0 RD, 0.59 (0.60) kpc for 0 PD, 0.51 (0.43) kpc for class 1, and 0.77 (0.70) kpc for class 2.
claims.finding: There is no clear relation between the molecular gas size R_CO and the morphological/dynamical galaxy type.

evidence.loc: No relation between the molecular size and the morphological type
evidence.quote: We can thus claim that no relation has been found between the molecular size, R$_{CO}$, and the galaxy types.

evidence.loc: Ionized (H$\alpha$) and stellar emissions in LIRGs: relations with the molecular distribution
evidence.quote: On the other hand, the molecular gas size does not seem to depend on the specific type of galaxy, remaining constant ($\sim$0.7 kpc) among the different subgroups (see § [5.2](#rco_morpho)).

claims.hypothesis: Local LIRGs represent an evolutionary link transforming gas-rich Spirals into intermediate-mass Early-Type Galaxies (ETGs).
claims.experiment: Compare M_star, SFR, R_CO, and R_star of the 24 local LIRGs against low-z Spirals (EDGE-CALIFA, PHANGS-ALMA), ETGs (ATLAS3D), and ULIRGs.
claims.result: LIRGs have M_star ~ 5e10 M_sun, R_star ~ 2.4 kpc, and R_CO ~ 0.7 kpc, matching ETGs (R_star ~ 2.2 kpc, R_CO ~ 1.0 kpc) while being ~6 times more compact in R_CO and ~1.6 times more compact in R_star than Spirals.
claims.finding: LIRGs are indistinguishable from ETGs in the M_star-R_star plane and have similar R_CO, supporting the scenario where LIRGs transform Spirals into Ellipticals.

evidence.quote: LIRGs are indistinguishable from ETGs in the M$_{star}$-R$_{star}$ plane, sharing a similar range in their stellar mass and size. However, LIRGs have a stellar host more compact than that of local Spirals, by a factor 1.6. This seems to support the evolutionary scenario in which LIRGs can transform Spirals to Ellipticals

claims.hypothesis: Low-z LIRGs are local analogs of high-z (1 < z < 6) main-sequence SFGs and SMGs in the spatial distribution of their star-forming ISM.
claims.experiment: Compare R_star, R_CO, R_cont, R_Halpha, and M_star of the local LIRGs with literature samples of high-z MS SFGs, cSFGs, and SMGs.
claims.result: While LIRGs have stellar masses and sizes similar to z~1-4 MS SFGs (factor 1.3 smaller R_star), their molecular sizes are ~2.6 times smaller than high-z SFGs and ~7.8 times smaller than SMGs, with median R_star/R_CO = 3.3 in LIRGs vs 1.8 and 1.2 in high-z SFGs and SMGs.
claims.finding: Although low-z LIRGs and high-z MS SFGs have similar stellar host masses and sizes, star formation in local LIRGs is centrally concentrated in the inner kpc whereas in high-z SFGs and SMGs it is much more extended across the host galaxy.

evidence.quote: Contrary to high-z SFGs and SMGs, which have comparable molecular and stellar sizes (median R$_{star}$/R$_{CO}$ = 1.8 and 1.2, respectively), the molecular gas in local LIRGs is more centrally concentrated (median R$_{star}$/R$_{CO}$ = 3.3).

These results indicate that while low-z LIRGs and high-z *MS*-SFGs have similar stellar masses and sizes, the regions of current star formation (traced by the ionized gas) and of potential star-formation (traced by the molecular gas) are substantially smaller in LIRGs, and constrained to the central kpc region.

why_this_data.value: ALMA high-resolution observations (<100 pc) resolve molecular emission in local LIRGs at giant molecular cloud (GMC) scales with high S/N, while combining extended and compact configurations provides a 3-5 kpc maximum recoverable scale.

evidence.quote: With the advent of high resolution instrument as the Atacama Large Millimeter/Submillimeter Array (ALMA), we are now able to study the molecular emission in local galaxies at spatial resolution similar to that covered by typical giant molecular cloud (GMCs, $\sim$100 pc).
A combination of the extended and compact configurations was used to achieve the 0.2$''$ angular resolution and a maximum recoverable scale of 10$''$-12$''$ (3-5 kpc).

why_this_method.value: The curve-of-growth (CoG) method in circular apertures is robust for galaxies with irregular or clumpy emission (such as interacting and merger systems) where parametric surface brightness fits like GALFIT fail, and is commonly applied at both low and high redshift.

evidence.quote: However, if the galaxies show irregular or clumpy emission (as in the case of interacting or merger systems) the half-light radii can be obtained from the `CoG` of the flux at increasingly large apertures.

In our specific case, we consider `CoG` method (i.e., the flux emission contained in circular apertures of increasing size are derived to compute the radius within which half of the total emission is contained) as a robust way to derive the R$_{eff}$ and it is commonly applied both at low- and high-z.

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: GALFIT parametric surface brightness fitting and the 'A/2' pixel-area method were considered as alternative size measurement methods; CoG was selected for the primary analysis and an empirical conversion was derived from A/2 to CoG.

evidence.quote: To derive the size of a system, different methodologies can be applied: `GALFIT`, the curve-of-growth `(CoG)` and the so-called `‘A/2’` methods can be used according to the objects considered.

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Elliptical apertures vs circular apertures for CoG; circular apertures were adopted after testing showed agreement within 5-12%.

evidence.quote: We considered that an equivalent circular aperture as a good approximation of the (major) elliptical aperture.
In the first case, the difference between the effective radius derived using a circular or elliptical aperture agrees within 5% while in the latter the difference agrees within 12%.

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Deconvolving the beam and applying inclination corrections to R_eff were considered and rejected because the effects are small (<1% for CO beam, ~1.05 in K-band for inclination).

evidence.quote: The CO(2–1) and 1.3 mm continuum sizes presented in this work are observed, that is, not corrected for the beam. The intrinsic CO and 1.3 mm continuum sizes are also resolved (larger than the beam) and (on average) smaller than the observed size by $\lesssim$1% and $\lesssim$4%, respectively.

evidence.loc: Extinction impact: optical *versus* near-IR ionized gas tracers. Inclination effects.
evidence.quote: Under this assumption, we also expect a small conversion at longer (mm) wavelengths: for this reason, no inclination correction has been applied to our sample.

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: ALMA 1.3 mm continuum effective radii were measured but excluded from the physical discussion because SED fitting showed 2-15x flux loss of faint extended emission due to sensitivity limits.

evidence.quote: With that in mind, we assume that the effective radii estimation of the 1.3 mm continuum emission is affected by the flux loss of the outer regions at this frequency: for this reason, we will not discuss the results derived for this tracer.

limitations_admitted.value: ALMA 1.3 mm continuum observations at >5 sigma miss a large fraction (<70%, Flux(SED)/Flux(ALMA) ~ 2-15) of faint extended dust emission due to surface brightness sensitivity limits, biasing R_cont to smaller values.

evidence.quote: The 1.3 mm continuum fluxes derived with ALMA at $>$5$\sigma$ are well below the SED emission (Flux(SED)/Flux(ALMA)$\sim$2-15) as a result of the sensitivity effects, for which the faint emission at larger radii is not observed.

evidence.loc: IR SED fit: ALMA flux loss estimation at 1.3 mm
evidence.quote: The gap between the two values clearly suggests that a considerable part of the 1.3 mm emission ($<$70%) is not detected by our ALMA observations.

limitations_admitted.value: Limited VIMOS FoV (~30''x30'') causes H-alpha effective radii for extended galaxies to be lower limits.

evidence.quote: For extended objects, the limited VIMOS FoV only allowed a lower limit to the R$_{eff}$ estimation to be derived.

limitations_admitted.value: 2MASS K-band images have low angular resolution (~2''), whereas HST/NICMOS images have high resolution (0.15'') but a small FoV (~19.5''x19.5'') that can underestimate sizes in extended systems and may miss diffuse Pa-alpha emission.

evidence.quote: 2MASS images do not have any limitation by the FoV although they are characterized by a low angular resolution ($\sim$2$''$).

evidence.loc: Extinction impact: optical *versus* near-IR ionized gas tracers. Inclination effects.
evidence.quote: However, *NICMOS/HST* images may be insensitive to diffuse Pa$\alpha$ emission (e.g., (cite: AAH06; Calzetti07))

limitations_admitted.value: The number of high-z galaxies with simultaneous high-resolution measurements of molecular, dust, ionized, and stellar sizes is still small.

evidence.loc: LIRGs *versus* high-z SFGs. Sizes of the (un)obscured star formation traced by molecular and ionized ISM
evidence.quote: Up to now, the number of high-z galaxies with available measurements of the molecular, ionized and stellar light distributions is quite low, such that the relations found here should be investigated further with larger samples to draw firm conclusions.

referee_caveats_inferred: In Table 4, the units for CO(2-1) Flux(R_eff) are printed in the column header as [Jy], whereas integrated line fluxes are normally in Jy km s^-1; a reproducer must verify whether these values are velocity-integrated fluxes (Jy km s^-1) mislabeled as Jy.
The outer radius used to define 100% of the flux in the curve-of-growth (CoG) method is not explicitly specified for each galaxy, though emission >5 sigma is selected.

reproducibility.score_reason: All 5 ALMA project codes, target coordinates, redshifts, distances, beam sizes, sensitivities, channel widths, and weighting are explicitly tabulated, and the curve-of-growth method with 4/5/6-sigma thresholds is clearly described. Minor deductions for unstated moment-0 integration windows, exact aperture center coordinates, and line-free channel ranges.
